title: Question 6
stem:
Fig. 6.1 shows a circuit that rectifies an alternating input voltage $V_{IN}$ and produces an output voltage $V_{OUT}$ across a resistor $R$.

{{figure:figure_6_1}}

Fig. 6.1

The four terminals of the rectification circuit are labelled $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$.
A capacitor $C$ is connected in parallel with resistor $R$.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by rectification.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what goes into the box in Fig. 6.1 and what comes out - compare the nature of $V_{IN}$ which alternates in direction with the one-directional $V_{OUT}$ needed for d.c. devices.
parts.proper_answer: Rectification is the conversion of alternating current (a.c.) to direct current (d.c.).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a.c. and d.c. mean**
Think of a.c. as current that repeatedly reverses direction as the voltage swings positive then negative. Direct current flows in one direction only. A rectifier lets you power d.c. circuits from the a.c. mains.

Step 2: **Link to Fig. 6.1**
$V_{IN}$ is alternating, $V_{OUT}$ across R is kept in one direction by the rectification circuit. So you can state it simply as conversion from a.c. to d.c.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Look at where C is connected in Fig. 6.1 - in parallel with R - and recall what a capacitor does when the rectified voltage tries to fall toward zero.
parts.proper_answer: To smooth the rectified output, reducing ripple to give a steadier d.c. voltage.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Role of a parallel capacitor**
A capacitor charges up to the peak voltage then discharges slowly through R when the rectified supply falls. It stores charge at the peaks and releases it in the troughs.

Step 2: **Why it matters**
Without C the output would fall to zero every half-cycle. With C it stays high, so the variation or ripple is much smaller. That is called smoothing.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
The variation of $V_{IN}$ with $t$ can be represented by

$$V_{IN} = A \cos Bt$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

Determine the values of $A$ and $B$. Give a unit with your answer for $A$.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the dashed $V_{IN}$ curve in Fig. 6.2 - read its maximum value at $t = 0$ for $A$, and measure the time for one full cosine cycle to get the period $T$.
Hint 2: Recall how angular frequency links to period for a cosine wave, $$B = \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$, and check that $T$ is converted from ms to s before calculating.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find A from the amplitude**
$V_{IN} = A \cos Bt$ has maximum $A$ at $t=0$ because $\cos 0 = 1$. From Fig. 6.2 the dashed curve starts at $$V_{IN} = 12\text{ V}$$ so $$A = 12\text{ V}$$

Step 2: **Find T then B**
The dashed $V_{IN}$ completes one full cycle from $0$ to $20\text{ ms}$. So $$T = 20 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$$ Angular frequency is $$B = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{20 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 3.1 \times 10^{2}\text{ rad s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the type of rectification produced by the circuit in Fig. 6.1.
hints: Hint 1: Compare how often $V_{OUT}$ reaches a peak with how often $V_{IN}$ reaches a positive peak - count the $V_{OUT}$ humps between 0 and 20 ms.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the frequency doubling**
$V_{IN}$ has period $20\text{ ms}$, but $V_{OUT}$ peaks at $0, 10, 20, 30\text{ ms}$. That is a peak every $10\text{ ms}$, twice as often as the input.

Step 2: **Interpret the meaning**
Both the positive and negative half-cycles of input are turned into positive output pulses. That only happens with full-wave rectification. Half-wave would give one pulse per $20\text{ ms}$.

parts.label: (b)(iii)

markscheme_points.text: four diodes shown, with correct circuit symbols
four diodes correctly connected to form a bridge rectifier

hints: Hint 1: Recall how many diodes are needed for full-wave operation with a single a.c. input - think of the diamond bridge with W and X at opposite corners and Y and Z at the other two corners.
Hint 2: Think about current direction - diodes must all point so that conventional current entering either W or X is always steered to leave via the same output terminal Y, and return via Z.
parts.proper_answer: Four diodes connected as a bridge rectifier between W, X and Y, Z with correct forward directions to give one-directional output.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Draw the diamond**
Join W to Y and to Z with a diode in each branch, and X to Y and to Z with a diode in each branch. That makes four diodes forming a bridge.

Step 2: **Get the directions right**
Arrange them so Y is always positive relative to Z. For example, diodes point toward Y from W and X, and point away from Z toward W and X. Then whichever way $V_{IN}$ pushes current in at W or X, it flows out at Y, through the external circuit, and back in at Z. Use proper diode triangle-and-bar symbols.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: Determine a value for the time constant for the discharge of the capacitor $C$ through the resistor $R$ in Fig. 6.1.

markscheme_points.text: V = V0 exp (−t / τ) or V = V0 exp (−t / RC) and τ = RC

hints: Hint 1: Identify the discharge section on the solid $V_{OUT}$ curve - from a 12 V peak where the capacitor starts to discharge through R until the next rectified pulse recharges it.
Hint 2: Pick two clear readings from that decay, e.g. $V_0 = 12\text{ V}$ at the peak and $V \approx 8.0\text{ V}$ after a time $t \approx 7.3\text{ ms}$, to use in the exponential law.
Hint 3: Set up $$V = V_0 e^{-t/\tau}$$ with your $V$, $V_0$ and $t$ values and solve for $\tau$ by taking natural logs.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Write the discharge law**
Between pulses the capacitor discharges through R, so $$V = V_0 e^{-t/\tau}$$ where $\tau = RC$ is the time constant, $V_0$ is the voltage at the start of decay and $t$ is time since then.

Step 2: **Read V0, V and t from Fig. 6.2**
Take $V_0 = 12\text{ V}$ at a peak, e.g. $t = 0$. The curve falls to about $$V = 8.0\text{ V}$$ just before the next rise, after $$t \approx 7.3 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$$ So $$8.0 = 12 \exp\left(\frac{-7.3 \times 10^{-3}}{\tau}\right)$$

Step 3: **Solve for tau**
Rearrange: $$\frac{8.0}{12} = e^{-t/\tau}$$ $$\ln\left(\frac{8}{12}\right) = \frac{-t}{\tau}$$ $$\tau = \frac{-7.3 \times 10^{-3}}{\ln(0.667)} \approx 1.8 \times 10^{-2}\text{ s}$$ That is about $0.018\text{ s}$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The capacitor $C$ has a capacitance of $570 \mu\text{F}$.

Use your answer in (b)(iv) to determine the resistance of resistor $R$.
hints: Hint 1: Recall the simple link between time constant $\tau$, resistance $R$ and capacitance $C$ for a resistor-capacitor discharge.
Hint 2: Convert the $570\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ capacitance to farads ($\times 10^{-6}$) and rearrange to find $R$ from your $\tau$ value in (b)(iv).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use tau = RC**
For discharge through R, $$\tau = RC$$ so $$R = \frac{\tau}{C}$$

Step 2: **Insert numbers**
With $\tau \approx 0.018\text{ s}$ and $$C = 570\text{ }\mu\text{F} = 570 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$$ $$R = \frac{0.018}{570 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 32\text{ }\Omega$$
